title: Ad Monimum Libri Tres
author: Fulgentius of Ruspe
source: Translated by Claude from stoa0128b.stoa001.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

passages.original: Non enim timet formidine criminis, sed robore puritalis et firmitate virtutis. Exigis a me præterea debitum, quod me celeriter, Domino adjuvane, spondeo redditurum. Non enim hoc debitum sic profiteor quemadmodum de quodam tuus Maro memorat, quod ipse fatebatur, sed reddere posse negabat: sed illud (al. illo) me debere fateor, in quo me reddere posse non nego, sed spondeo. Ipse enim mihi donat unde reddam, qui donavit ut debeam. Nisi enim ab illo acciperemus, non solum reddere, sed nec ipsum debere possemus.
passages.english: For it fears not from dread of guilt, but from the strength of purity and the firmness of virtue. You demand of me, moreover, a debt, which I promise that I will repay quickly, with the Lord's help. For I do not acknowledge this debt in the way your Virgil records of a certain man, who confessed it but denied that he could repay it; rather, I confess that I owe that [debt] in which I do not deny that I can repay, but promise [to repay]. For he who granted that I should owe gives me the means to repay. For unless we received from him, we could not only not repay, but could not even owe.
passages.notes: "puritalis" read as "puritatis"; "adjuvane" as "adjuvante". "Maro" is Virgil. "(al. illo)" is an editorial variant reading. "in quo me reddere posse non nego" is taken as "in which I do not deny that I can repay"; the Latin is compressed.

passages.original: Atque ut tuus sermo praefati sancti viri fulciretur eloquo, eadem verba, quae a beato Augustino (de Perfect. justitiæ, cap. 13) sunt dicta, subnectens: Ait enim, inquis, idem gloriosissimus Augustinus: De illo enim bono dictum hic debemus accipere, quod ibi ait: Deus de coelo prospexit super filios hominum, ut videat 5 si est intelligens, aut requirens Deum (Psal. XIII, 2). Hoc ergo bonum, quod eat requirere Deum, non erat qui faceret, non erat usque ad unum, sed in eo ,eMere hominum quod prædestinatum eat ad interitum. Hic dicta sancti Augustini determinans, et ad me intentionem tuarum dirigens litterarum, dicis sentire me jam cur iterum haec inculces, scilicet quod sæpius reluctanti te mihi, praedestinationem non tantum in bono dici, sed etiam in malo, dum in malo prædestinationem te relegisse diceres, ipse docens aiebam ad poenam debitam, non ad malum facien- dum, posse dici aliam prædestinationem.
passages.english: And so that your argument might be supported by the words of the aforesaid holy man, you append the same words that were spoken by the blessed Augustine (On the Perfection of Justice, ch. 13). For, you say, the same most glorious Augustine says: "For here we ought to take [it as] said of that good of which it says there: God looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see if there is anyone who understands or seeks God (Ps. 13:2). This good, then, which is to seek God, there was none who did, not even one, but in that kind of men which is predestined to destruction." Concluding with these words of saint Augustine, and directing the aim of your letter at me, you say that I now perceive why you press these things on me again: namely because, when you repeatedly resisted me [in saying] that predestination is spoken of not only in good but also in evil, since you said you had read of predestination in evil, I myself, instructing [you], used to say that another predestination could be spoken of with respect to deserved punishment, not to doing evil.
passages.notes: Scanning errors: "eat" read as "est"; "eMere" as "genere"; "facien- dum" as "faciendum". The syntax of the final sentence ("quod sæpius reluctanti te mihi...") is awkward; it has been rendered by sense.

passages.original: Quamvis igitur tu ipse, caeterique tui similes studio legendi, vel velocitate intelligendi, ex hoc loco dictorum sancti Augustini, quæ in tua epistola posuisli, facillime cognoscatis, quid catholicus habeat intellectus de his quos ad interitum prædestinatos audimus, tamen ne tardiores quique hunc tantum locum minus sibi putent in hac quaestione sufiicere, de aliis quoque sancti Augustini libris quaedam inserui, quibus docuit humanae iniquitatis causam solam esse superbiam, nec ad peccandum homines, sed ad damnationem pradestinatos a Deo, qui ut non adjuventur a Deo, in ipsis causa est, non in Deo. In libro itaque secundo de Baptismo parvulorum ad Marcellinum scribens, inter alia sic dicit (Cap.
passages.english: Although, then, you yourself and others like you, through zeal in reading or quickness of understanding, would very easily recognise from this passage of saint Augustine's words, which you placed in your letter, what Catholic understanding holds concerning those whom we hear [called] predestined to destruction, nevertheless, so that slower readers may not think this one passage insufficient for them on this question, I have also inserted some things from other books of saint Augustine. In these he taught that pride alone is the cause of human iniquity, and that men are predestined by God not to sin but to damnation, and that the cause of their not being helped by God lies in themselves, not in God. And so, writing to Marcellinus in the second book On the Baptism of Infants, he says among other things as follows (ch.
passages.notes: Scanning errors: "posuisli" read as "posuisti", "sufiicere" as "sufficere", "pradestinatos" as "prædestinatos". The chapter reference continues in the following passage.

passages.original: Non autem ignoras etiam præterito tempore illi luculentissimo sancti Augustini operi, quod scripsit de prædestinatione sanctorum, a quibusdam Gallis objectum, quod beatus Augustinus in assertione praedestinationis divinæ, peccatores, non ad solum prædestinatos diceret judicium, sed etiam ad peccatum;
passages.english: Nor are you unaware that in time past also, objection was raised by certain Gauls against that most brilliant work of saint Augustine which he wrote On the Predestination of the Saints: [namely] that the blessed Augustine, in asserting divine predestination, said that sinners were predestined not only to judgement but also to sin;
passages.notes: The sentence continues in the following passage.

passages.original: < Spiritus autem sanctus, quod in sola catholica Ecclesia per manus impositionem dari dicitur, nimirum hoc intelligi majores nostri voluerunt quod Apostolus ait: Quoniam caritas Det diffusa est in cordibus nostris, per Spiritum sanctum qui datus est nobis. » Subsequenter autem etiam, quod Judas apostolus in Epistola sua posuit, remoto dubitationis ambiguo, sanctus Augustinus exposuit. Judas enim apostolus dicit: Hi sunt qui segregant semetipsos, animales, Spiritum non habentes. Et beatus Auguslinus de caritate Dei, quae diffusa est in cordibus nostris per Spiritum sanctum, qui datus est nobis, dicit: < Ipsa est enim caritas quam non habent qui ab Ecclesiae catholicæ communione præcisi sunt.
passages.english: "But as for the Holy Spirit's being said to be given only in the Catholic Church through the laying on of hands, our forebears doubtless wished this to be understood as what the Apostle says: Because the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us." Then, subsequently, saint Augustine also expounded, removing all ambiguity of doubt, what the apostle Jude set down in his Epistle. For the apostle Jude says: These are those who separate themselves, natural men, not having the Spirit. And the blessed Augustine says of the love of God which has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us: "For this is the love which those do not have who have been cut off from the communion of the Catholic Church.
passages.notes: Scanning errors: "Det" read as "Dei", "Auguslinus" as "Augustinus"; "<" taken as an opening quotation mark.

passages.original: Quod consilium in epistola quam ad te nuper scripsi ad illud pertinere memora- vi quod, duobus denariis a Domino acceptis, fidelis stabularius supererogavit (Luc. x, 35). Cujus loci sensum , licet non ita a sancto Augustino positum asseras , alios tamen illustres viros taliter hoc posuisse confirmas. Est quidem verum : quia sanctus Augustinus hoc dixit ab Apostolo supererogatum, quod cum secundum præceptum posset, si vellet, de Evangelio vivere, maluit tamen non solum sibi, sed et his qui cum illo erant, propriis manibus laborare, sicut Ephesiis veraciter dixit: Ipsi scitis , quoniam (al.
passages.english: This counsel, in the letter I recently wrote to you, I mentioned as pertaining to what the faithful innkeeper spent beyond [what was required] after receiving two denarii from the Lord (Luke 10:35). Though you maintain that the sense of this passage was not given thus by saint Augustine, you nonetheless affirm that other illustrious men have given it thus. It is indeed true: for saint Augustine said that what the Apostle spent beyond [what was required] was this, that though according to the precept he could, if he wished, live from the Gospel, he preferred nevertheless to labour with his own hands not only for himself but also for those who were with him, as he truthfully said to the Ephesians: You yourselves know that (al.
passages.notes: The variant note "(al." is completed in the following passage. In the parable it is the Samaritan who gives the innkeeper two denarii; the text loosely says "from the Lord".

passages.original: Nam et ipsi sancti, quorum ministerio Deus Scripturarum suarum dignatus est aperire secreta, dixerunt pleraque non uno modo tantum, sed multipliciter, sine offensione duntaxat veræ Mei non indecenter intelligi. Sicut ipse beatus Augustinus in mysterio arcae Noe fecisse cognoscitur adversus Faustum : namque Manichæo as- serente, in libris Veteris Testamenti nihil de Christi in carne vera futuro adventu prophetice contineri, ostendens idem beatissimus Augustinus nostram veterem Scripturam propheticis de Christo significatio- nibus plenam, et ob hoc divinitus inspiratam, sic inter cætera illud exponit, quod memoratam arcam bicameratam et tricameratam Deus imperat construendam, ut in libro de Civitate Dei quintodecimo, duobus aliis modis ejusdem loci mysticam explanationem, non doctis humanæ sapientiae verbis , sed vere (sicut Apostolus dicit) in doctrina spiritus, non minus dulciter quam mirabiliter explicarit. Quod ut facilius agnoscatur, utriusque operis, sicut ab eo posita sunt, verba subnectam. Igitur adversus Faustum posuit haec: « Quod inrenora arcæ bicamerata et tricamerata construuntur, sicut ex omnibus gentibus vel bipartitam multitudinem congregat Ecclesia, propter circumcisionem et præputium, vel tripartitam propter tres filios Noe, quorum progenie repletus est orbis.
passages.english: For the saints themselves too, through whose ministry God deigned to open the secrets of his Scriptures, said many things that could fittingly be understood not in one way only but in many, provided only that there is no offence to the true faith. So the blessed Augustine himself is known to have done regarding the mystery of Noah's ark, against Faustus. For when the Manichaean asserted that nothing is contained prophetically in the books of the Old Testament about Christ's future coming in true flesh, this same most blessed Augustine, showing that our old Scripture is full of prophetic signs of Christ, and for this reason divinely inspired, expounds among other things God's command that the said ark be built with two and three storeys. In the fifteenth book of The City of God he likewise explained the mystical interpretation of the same passage in two other ways, not in words taught by human wisdom but truly, as the Apostle says, in the teaching of the Spirit, no less sweetly than wonderfully. So that this may be more easily recognised, I will append the words of both works as he set them down. Against Faustus, then, he set down these: "That the lower parts of the ark are built with two storeys and three storeys [signifies] that the Church gathers from all nations a multitude either twofold, because of circumcision and uncircumcision, or threefold, because of the three sons of Noah, by whose offspring the world was filled.
passages.notes: Scanning errors: "Mei" read as "fidei"; "inrenora" probably "inferiora" (lower parts). "ut in libro" has been read as introducing a further statement ("likewise"); the syntax is loose.

passages.original: Rursus idem beatus Augustinus in libro primo (Cap. 3) de Trinitate asserit utile esse plures libros a pluribus fieri diverso stylo, non diversa fide, etiam de quæstionibus eisdem, ut ad plurimos res ipsa perveniat, ad alios sic, ad alios autem sic. Si ergo illa, quae de arca Noe beatus Augustinus uno loco duobus posuit modis, a duobus hominibus singula assumpta singulis ponantur in locis, nonne uterque digne tenai pronuntiabitur veritatis ; si tamen sic uterque unum horum suis inditum dictis videatur astruere, ut illud quod aliter in suis dictis aeque veritati congruum ponit, magis pacatus approbet quam contentiosus impugnet.
passages.english: Again, the same blessed Augustine asserts in the first book (ch. 3) of On the Trinity that it is useful for several books to be written by several people, in different style but not different faith, even on the same questions, so that the matter itself may reach as many as possible, some in this way and others in that. If, then, the things that blessed Augustine set down about Noah's ark in two ways in one place were taken up separately by two men and set down each in a separate place, will not each be declared a worthy holder of the truth? Provided, however, that each appears to maintain the one [interpretation] set down in his own words in such a way that he approves, peaceably rather than contentiously attacking, the one that the other sets down differently in his words, equally consistent with truth.
passages.notes: "tenai" read as "tenax" (holder, one who holds fast).
